intro: From cave paintings to comic books, France has influenced how the world eats, dresses, paints, writes and watches films. Its culture is also proudly regional, with each area guarding its own food and traditions.

chapters.title: Food
text: In 2010 UNESCO listed the 'gastronomic meal of the French' as part of the world's cultural heritage: a long meal with several courses, shared with family or friends. In 2022 the craft of making the baguette was added too.

Every region has its own dishes: crêpes from Brittany, choucroute (sauerkraut with sausages) from Alsace, bouillabaisse fish stew from Marseille and cassoulet, a slow-cooked bean stew, from the south-west. France makes hundreds of kinds of cheese, from soft Camembert to blue Roquefort.
Even some 'French' classics have foreign roots. The croissant was inspired by the kipferl, a crescent-shaped bread from Austria.

chapters.title: Art and museums
text: The Louvre in Paris is the most visited art museum in the world. It holds the Mona Lisa, painted by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci, who spent his last years in France.

In the 1870s a group of painters including Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Berthe Morisot began painting outdoors, capturing light and movement with quick brushstrokes. A critic mocked Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, and the name stuck: Impressionism.
In the early 1900s Paris was the centre of the art world. Artists from everywhere, such as the Spaniard Pablo Picasso, came to work there alongside French painters like Henri Matisse.

chapters.title: Books and big ideas
text: France has more Nobel Prizes in Literature than any other country. Famous writers include Molière, whose comedies are still performed, Victor Hugo, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, and Jules Verne, who imagined submarines and trips to the Moon long before they existed.

French thinkers have shaped ideas around the world, from Descartes ('I think, therefore I am') to Enlightenment writers like Voltaire and Rousseau and, in the 1900s, Simone de Beauvoir, a pioneer of feminism.

chapters.title: Cinema, comics and music
text: On 28 December 1895 the Lumière brothers held one of the first public film screenings for a paying audience, in a café in Paris. Georges Méliès soon followed with special effects, including A Trip to the Moon in 1902. The Cannes Film Festival, held since 1946, is the most famous film festival in the world.

Comics, called bandes dessinées, are treated as a serious art form, sometimes called 'the ninth art'. Astérix, created in 1959, is about a village of Gauls holding out against Julius Caesar, and the town of Angoulême hosts a huge comics festival every January.

French music ranges from the chansons of Édith Piaf to the electronic music of Daft Punk. Every 21 June since 1982, the Fête de la Musique fills streets with free concerts by anyone who wants to play.

chapters.title: Landmarks and fashion
text: The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair. Many Parisians first thought it was ugly, but it was the tallest structure in the world until 1930 and is now a symbol of France.
In April 2019 a fire destroyed the roof and spire of Notre-Dame cathedral. After five years of work by hundreds of craftspeople, it reopened in December 2024.
Paris is one of the world's fashion capitals. Designers such as Coco Chanel and Christian Dior changed how people dressed, and Paris Fashion Week is one of the biggest events in the fashion calendar.

cardGroups.title: Films to know

items.title: A Trip to the Moon
items.subtitle: 1902 · Georges Méliès
items.text: Rocket scientists land in the eye of the Man in the Moon: one of the first science-fiction films.

items.title: The 400 Blows
items.subtitle: 1959 · François Truffaut
items.text: A troubled Paris schoolboy runs away; a landmark of the French 'New Wave'.

items.title: Amélie
items.subtitle: 2001 · Jean-Pierre Jeunet
items.text: A shy Paris café waitress secretly sets out to make other people happy.

items.title: The Intouchables
items.subtitle: 2011 · Olivier Nakache and Éric Toledano
items.text: The true-story friendship between a wealthy man who is paralysed and his carer, one of France's biggest hits.

items.title: The Artist
items.subtitle: 2011 · Michel Hazanavicius
items.text: A silent, black-and-white film that became the first French production to win the Oscar for Best Picture.

items.title: Anatomy of a Fall
items.subtitle: 2023 · Justine Triet
items.text: A courtroom drama that won the top prize at Cannes and an Oscar for its screenplay.

cardGroups.intro: A starter list across more than a century of French cinema.

items.title: The Three Musketeers
items.subtitle: 1844 · Alexandre Dumas
items.text: D'Artagnan joins three swordsmen in adventures at the court of Louis XIII.

items.title: Les Misérables
items.subtitle: 1862 · Victor Hugo
items.text: Ex-prisoner Jean Valjean tries to build a new life while a policeman hunts him; later a famous musical.

items.title: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas
items.subtitle: 1870 · Jules Verne
items.text: Captain Nemo's submarine, the Nautilus, explores the oceans long before real submarines could.

items.title: The Little Prince
items.subtitle: 1943 · Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
items.text: A pilot stranded in the desert meets a boy from a tiny planet; one of the most translated books in the world.

items.title: Astérix
items.subtitle: from 1959 · Goscinny and Uderzo
items.text: A village of Gauls, powered by a magic potion, holds out against Julius Caesar's Romans.

items.title: Clair de lune
items.subtitle: Claude Debussy
items.text: A gentle, dreamy piano piece, one of the most famous in classical music.

items.title: La Vie en rose
items.subtitle: Édith Piaf, 1947
items.text: The signature song of France's most famous singer.

items.title: One More Time
items.subtitle: Daft Punk, 2000
items.text: The Paris duo in robot helmets helped make French electronic music famous worldwide.

items.title: Djadja
items.subtitle: Aya Nakamura, 2018
items.text: A global hit that made Aya Nakamura one of the most-streamed French-language singers.

items.title: Croissant
items.subtitle: Everywhere
items.text: A buttery crescent pastry, inspired by an Austrian bread.

items.title: Crêpes
items.subtitle: Brittany
items.text: Thin pancakes; savoury buckwheat galettes are the Breton classic.

items.title: Bouillabaisse
items.subtitle: Marseille
items.text: A fish stew flavoured with saffron and served with garlic sauce.

items.title: Ratatouille
items.subtitle: Provence
items.text: Slow-cooked summer vegetables: aubergine, courgette, peppers and tomatoes.

items.title: Choucroute
items.subtitle: Alsace
items.text: Sauerkraut with sausages and pork, showing German influence.

items.title: Macarons
items.subtitle: Paris
items.text: Colourful almond biscuits with a creamy filling.

items.name: Galette des Rois
items.text: Families share an almond cake hiding a tiny charm; whoever finds it is king or queen for the day.

items.name: Nice Carnival
items.text: Giant floats and flower battles fill the streets of Nice.

items.name: Easter
items.text: Children are told the church bells fly to Rome and return with chocolate eggs.

items.name: Cannes Film Festival
items.text: Stars gather on the Riviera for the world's most famous film festival.

items.name: Fête de la Musique
items.text: On 21 June anyone can play music in the street, in towns all over France.

items.name: Bastille Day
items.text: 14 July brings a military parade in Paris and fireworks everywhere; the Tour de France races on.

items.name: Heritage Days
items.text: Palaces, ministries and historic buildings open their doors to the public for free.

items.name: Armistice Day
items.text: On 11 November France remembers the end of the First World War.

items.name: Festival of Lights
items.text: Lyon glows with candles in windows and light shows on buildings; Christmas markets open in Alsace.
